books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Henry Clay, resolutions offered in the Senate, January 29, 1850
Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850
John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, March 4, 1850
Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18 (1849)

An Act proposing to the State of Texas the Establishment of her Northern and Western Boundaries, approved September 9, 1850

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Compromise of 1850 resolved the sectional conflict over slavery in the United States in the period 1848–1854.

documents.title: Clay proposes his compromise
documents.source: Henry Clay, resolutions offered in the Senate, January 29, 1850. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Clay, the Kentucky Whig senator who had brokered the Missouri Compromise thirty years earlier, offering his plan to settle every slavery question at once.
documents.text:
It being desirable, for the peace, concord, and harmony of the Union of these States, to settle and adjust amicably all existing questions of controversy between them arising out of the institution of slavery upon a fair, equitable and just basis: therefore,

1. Resolved, That California, with suitable boundaries, ought, upon her application to be admitted as one of the States of this Union, without the imposition by Congress of any restriction in respect to the exclusion or introduction of slavery within those boundaries.

2. Resolved, That as slavery does not exist by law, and is not likely to be introduced into any of the territory acquired by the United States from the republic of Mexico, it is inexpedient for Congress to provide by law either for its introduction into, or exclusion from, any part of the said territory; and that appropriate territorial governments ought to be established by Congress in all of the said territory, not assigned as the boundaries of the proposed State of California, without the adoption of any restriction or condition on the subject of slavery.

documents.title: Webster speaks for the Union
documents.source: Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850 (Congressional Globe Appendix — Webster's revised text). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Webster, the Massachusetts Whig senator, speaking for the compromise at the risk of his standing with antislavery voters at home.
documents.text:
Mr. President, — I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American, and a member of the Senate of the United States.

. . .

I speak to-day for the preservation of the Union. “Hear me for my cause.” I speak to-day, out of a solicitous and anxious heart, for the restoration to the country of that quiet and that harmony which make the blessings of this Union so rich and so dear to us all.

. . .

Desirous of immediate connection with the United States, [California's] Senators were appointed and representatives chosen, . . . asking, in behalf of their State, that the state may be admitted into this Union as one of the United States. This constitution, Sir, contains an express prohibition against slavery, or involuntary servitude, in the State of California. . . . This prohibition against slavery, it is said, was inserted with entire unanimity.

documents.title: Calhoun warns of disunion
documents.source: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by Senator James M. Mason, March 4, 1850. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Calhoun, the South Carolina senator and slavery's leading defender, too ill to speak himself; he died on March 31, 1850, before the compromise passed.
documents.text:
I have, Senators, believed from the first that the agitation of the subject of slavery would, if not prevented by some timely and effective measure, end in disunion.

. . .

To this question there can be but one answer, — that the immediate cause is the almost universal discontent which pervades all the States composing the Southern section of the Union.

. . .

It is a great mistake to suppose that disunion can be effected by a single blow. The cords which bind these States together in one common Union are far too numerous and powerful for that. Disunion must be the work of time.

. . .

I return to the question with which I commenced, How can the Union be saved? There is but one way by which it can with any certainty; and that is, by a full and final settlement, on the principle of justice, of all the questions at issue between the two sections.

documents.title: The Fugitive Slave Act
documents.source: Fugitive Slave Act, approved September 18, 1850 (Statutes at Large, vol. 9). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The fourth of the five compromise laws, written to give Southern claimants a federal process for recovering people who had escaped slavery.
documents.text:
Sec. 6. . . . In no trial or hearing under this act shall the testimony of such alleged fugitive be admitted in evidence; and the certificates in this and the first [fourth] section mentioned, shall be conclusive of the right of the person or persons in whose favor granted, to remove such fugitive to the State or Territory from which he escaped, and shall prevent all molestation of such person or persons by any process issued by any court, judge, magistrate, or other person whomsoever.

Sec. 8. . . . in all cases where the proceedings are before a commissioner, he shall be entitled to a fee of ten dollars in full for his services in each case, upon the delivery of the said certificate to the claimant, his agent or attorney; or a fee of five dollars in cases where the proof shall not, in the opinion of such commissioner, warrant such certificate and delivery, inclusive of all services incident to such arrest and examination, to be paid, in either case, by the claimant, his or her agent or attorney . . .

documents.title: California's constitution bans slavery
documents.source: Constitution of the State of California, Article I, Section 18, adopted 1849. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The constitution written by California's own convention at Monterey in 1849, as the territory rushed toward statehood.
documents.text: Neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated in this State.

documents.title: A warning to Black Bostonians
documents.source: “Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all,” broadside posted in Boston, April 24, 1851 (Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A street broadside posted by Boston abolitionists after the Fugitive Slave Act, warning Black residents that the city's own police had become slave catchers.
documents.text: Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all, You are hereby respectfully cautioned and advised, to avoid conversing with the Watchmen and Police Officers of Boston, For since the recent Order of the Mayor & Aldermen, they are empowered to act as Kidnappers and Slave Catchers, And they have already been actually employed in Kidnapping, Catching, and Keeping Slaves. Therefore, if you value your Liberty, and the Welfare of the Fugitives among you, Shun them in every possible manner, as so many Hounds on the track of the most unfortunate of your race. Keep a Sharp Look Out for Kidnappers, and have Top Eye open. April 24, 1851.

documents.title: Texas gives up land and takes ten million dollars
documents.source: An Act proposing to the State of Texas the Establishment of her Northern and Western Boundaries, approved September 9, 1850 (Statutes at Large, vol. 9). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The first of the five compromise laws, settling the boundary between Texas and New Mexico and paying Texas for the land it gave up.
documents.text:
FIRST. The State of Texas will agree that her boundary on the north shall commence at the point at which the meridian of one hundred degrees west from Greenwich is intersected by the parallel of thirty-six degrees thirty minutes north latitude, and shall run from said point due west to the meridian of one hundred and three degrees west from Greenwich; thence her boundary shall run due south to the thirty-second degree of north latitude; thence on the said parallel of thirty-two degrees of north latitude to the Rio Bravo del Norte, and thence with the channel of said river to the Gulf of Mexico.

. . .

FOURTH. The United States, in consideration of said establishment of boundaries, cession of claim to territory, and relinquishment of claims, will pay to the State of Texas the sum of ten millions of dollars in a stock bearing five per cent. interest, and redeemable at the end of fourteen years, the interest payable half-yearly at the treasury of the United States.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the Compromise of 1850 resolved the sectional conflict, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of resolution does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Mexican-American War, the Wilmot Proviso, or the sectional balance before 1850.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, the personal liberty laws, or Uncle Tom's Cabin.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of resolution, explaining why the settlement held in Congress but failed in the streets, or showing how the same compromise pulled in opposite directions.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The Compromise of 1850 resolved the sectional conflict in Congress but not in the country — it settled the map and the boundary lines, while its Fugitive Slave Act made the slavery question personal for Northerners and guaranteed the argument would return.
Context: The Mexican-American War added California and the Southwest in 1848, the Wilmot Proviso had already split Congress by section, and California's free-state constitution arrived in 1849 with the Senate balanced fifteen to fifteen.
Evidence: Documents 1, 2, and 5 show the settlement taking shape — Clay's resolutions, Webster's plea for the Union, and California banning slavery itself. Document 7 shows the boundary bargain working, with Texas paid ten million dollars for land it gave up. Documents 3, 4, and 6 show the settlement failing — Calhoun's demand for a final settlement, the Fugitive Slave Act's one-sided hearings, and a Boston broadside warning Black residents against their own police.
Beyond the documents: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 reopened the territorial question the compromise had postponed, and Northern personal liberty laws and Uncle Tom's Cabin spread resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act.
Sourcing: Clay wrote as a compromiser seeking a single settlement; Webster spoke as a Northerner risking his voters to save the Union; Calhoun wrote as a dying defender of slavery demanding a final settlement; the broadside was a street warning, not a law, and shows the act's effect on daily life.
Complexity: The compromise worked as legislation and failed as a settlement — the same law that admitted California free also put federal slave catchers on Northern streets, so the peace it bought in Congress was paid for with anger in the North.
